newsitem.title: FRANCE: Arafat to attend World Bank donors' meeting.
newsitem.headline: Arafat to attend World Bank donors' meeting.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat is to attend a donors' meeting of the World Bank's Consultative Group on the West Bank and Gaza in Paris on Wednesday, the Bank said on Monday.
The meeting is a pledging session for World Bank programmes in the autonomous Palestinian areas for 1997, Kemal Dervis, World Bank vice-president for the Middle East and North Africa, told reporters.
Arafat will be accompanied by Nabil Shaath and Mohammed Nashashibi, who are among his main advisers for economic and financial issues.
Arafat is to hold a news conference on Wednesday (1630 GMT) after the donors' meeting, which some 40 countries and international institutions are expected to attend.

The meeting takes place after a severe worsening of the economic situation in the West Bank and Gaza following Israel's decision to close off those areas in February after a wave of bomb attacks by Moslem fundamentalists killed dozens of people within Israel.
The World Bank said that the political situation had resulted in projections of a five percent decline of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) for 1996 in the autonomous Palestinian areas.
But Dervis said that, barring new political upheavals, "there is no reason that the Palestinian economy cannot do well.

"The bad situation is due to political and security constraints as well as uncertainty in the minds of potential investors. But this is not a situation that is so bad that it cannot work. Things can and do advance," he said.
A main hope for improvement is the expected opening in about two months of the al-Muntar industrial park on the Palestinian side of the Israel-Gaza Strip border, Dervis said.

Under optimal conditions, the project will employ 17,000 people directly, mostly in textiles, and 35,000 indirectly by early 1998. "That would definitely make things look better and it would be an example for another such park to be established at Rafah and others in the West Bank," he said.
But Dervis said much of the feasibility of the parks depended on relative freedom of movement of goods towards Israeli ports and of investors in and out of the Gaza Strip.
Referring to Israel's past sudden closures of Palestinian areas following terror attacks, Dervis said rules can be set to allow for trading while respecting Israel's security concerns.

"For example, that you have to declare what you are sending a week in advance and who is coming. What is important is that these measures are reasonable and efficient, that one uses modern methods of detection," he said.

"But especially, these measures should be predictable so that people can ajust to them. If the rules of the game are clear, the security measures may be a little irritant but will not prevent development from taking place. What is extremely damaging is unpredictability and changing the rules of the game week by week," he said.
A donors' meeting in Paris in January made pledges totalling $856 million. World Bank documents showed that at the end of August, commitments stood at $559 million and disbursements at $287 million.
